0.title: Course Introduction
0.content:
The theory lessons have built up knowledge of the Loire Valley's four sub-regions and dozens of AOCs; now it is time to make these abstract ideas visual. This lesson uses Mapbox GL JS + GeoJSON to present the Loire Valley's complete geographic structure interactively — you can see each AOC's boundaries, river courses and soil-zone distribution, and click to explore the details of each region.

Learning Objectives

🗺️ Geographic integration of the four sub-regions

Build spatial memory of Nantais → Anjou-Saumur → Touraine → Centre through the interactive map

🌊 River systems and microclimates

Observe how the Loire's main stem and tributaries such as the Maine, Layon, Vienne, Cher, Indre and Sèvre shape AOC boundaries

📐 AOC nesting relationships

Understand the geographic layering of multi-level AOCs such as Anjou → Anjou Villages → Savennières → Coulée de Serrant

🪨 Visualising soil zones

Use the map to understand the geological boundaries of Anjou Noir vs Anjou Blanc and Tuffeau vs Schist

2.content:
This site's Loire interactive map is rendered with Mapbox GL JS, with data from the official GeoJSON of France's INAO (the national appellations institute), combined with hand-corrected Cru-level boundaries. The map supports multi-level display and interactive exploration.

🌊 Layer 1: Sub-Region

  • Pays Nantais (blue): the Muscadet family, Gros Plant
  • Anjou-Saumur (purple): Anjou, Saumur, Layon, Bonnezeaux, Savennières, Saumur-Champigny
  • Touraine (brown): Vouvray, Montlouis, Chinon, Bourgueil, Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil
  • Centre-Loire (green): Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé, Menetou-Salon, Quincy, Reuilly

🍇 Layer 2: AOC (Appellation)

Shows specific AOC boundaries; click any AOC to pop up a detail card (area, varieties, soils, style, typical producers).

🏆 Layer 3: Cru (single vineyard / sub-AOC)

Shows Cru-level boundaries such as Coulée de Serrant, La Roche-aux-Moines, Bonnezeaux, Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru and Chaume Premier Cru.

🪨 Layer 4: Soil Zone

  • Tuffeau (shown in white)
  • Brioverian schist (shown in black)
  • Kimmeridgian marl (shown in golden yellow)
  • Silex flint (shown in dark red)
2.quiz.question: Which technology renders this site's Loire interactive map?
2.quiz.explanation: This site uses Mapbox GL JS (vector layers) with the official INAO GeoJSON data to render all the regional maps. Mapbox GL JS offers 60fps interaction, crisp vector zooming and highly customisable styling, and is currently the mainstream choice for wine-map visualisation.

7.title: Map-Reading Tips — Three Key Observations
7.highlights.0.title: Rivers as boundaries
7.highlights.0.content: The main Loire and tributaries Layon/Cher/Vienne often serve as AOC boundaries
7.highlights.1.title: South-facing slopes first
7.highlights.1.content: Top AOCs depend on sun-facing slopes, not on which bank of the river they lie: Savennières and Vouvray are on the north bank, Sancerre, Chinon and Montlouis on the south/west bank
7.highlights.2.title: Nested pyramid
7.highlights.2.content: Within a large AOC there are small AOCs, within small AOCs Crus, and within Crus single vineyards
7.content:
Learning to "read" a wine map matters more than memorising AOC names. The following three observation tips will help you quickly understand the structural logic of any wine region.

🌊 Observation 1: How rivers divide AOCs

AOC boundaries in the Loire Valley often follow river courses:

  • Main Loire: Vouvray (north bank) vs Montlouis (south bank), and Sancerre (left/west bank) vs Pouilly-Fumé (right/east bank) face each other across the river; Anjou Noir (west, schist) and Anjou Blanc (east, tuffeau) are geological zones, not divided by the river
  • Layon: the Layon sweet-wine belt follows the valley entirely
  • Vienne: Chinon lies in the Vienne valley, Bourgueil on the north bank of the main Loire
  • Cher: the broad Touraine AOC spans the Cher valley

🧭 Observation 2: Aspect (Exposure) determines quality

The ideal aspect for Northern Hemisphere wine is south-facing (exposé sud) — the most sunshine, the strongest photosynthesis and the best grape ripeness. Many of the Loire Valley's top AOCs lie on south-facing sunny slopes, whichever bank of the river they are on:

  • Savennières: steep south-facing slope on the north bank of the Loire
  • Vouvray: south-facing slope on the north bank of the Loire (east of Tours)
  • Sancerre: sunny slopes on the high ground of the left (west) bank of the Loire
  • Chinon, Saumur-Champigny, Montlouis: all on the south bank, likewise using sunny slopes and tuffeau

So the key is "the sun-facing side (aspect and slope)," not "which bank of the river."

📍 Observation 3: The nested pyramid structure

The French AOC system is a nested pyramid, and on the map the same vineyard may belong to several AOCs at once:

  • Savennières (village level) → about 145 hectares
  • ↳ La Roche-aux-Moines (Cru) → 33 hectares
  • ↳ Coulée de Serrant (single vineyard) → 7 hectares

Growers can choose which level to bottle under. The higher the level, the stricter the rules, the lower the yield and the higher the price.
7.quiz.question: In the Loire Valley, what determines quality more than "which bank of the river the vineyard is on"?
7.quiz.options.0: Whether the vineyard is on the north or south bank of the river
7.quiz.options.1: The vineyard's straight-line distance from the Atlantic
7.quiz.options.2: Aspect and slope — a south-facing, sunny sun-facing slope
7.quiz.options.3: The administrative district the vineyard belongs to
7.quiz.explanation: The ideal aspect for Northern Hemisphere vineyards is south-facing (exposé sud), because the sun shines obliquely from the south and the angle of incidence on a south-facing slope is close to 90°, giving the highest photosynthetic efficiency. Savennières, Vouvray and Bourgueil are on the north bank, Sancerre on the left (west) bank, and Chinon, Saumur-Champigny and Montlouis on the south bank — top AOCs lie on both banks of the river, and what they share is a south-facing sun-facing slope. When reading a regional map, look at aspect and slope first, then the river bank.
8.title: Level 4-2 Knowledge Check
8.questions.0.question: What is the order of the Loire Valley's four sub-regions from west to east?
8.questions.0.explanation: Starting from Nantes at the Atlantic outlet and going upstream along the Loire: Pays Nantais (maritime) → Anjou-Saumur (transitional) → Touraine (continental-transitional) → Centre-Loire (semi-continental). This west-to-east order corresponds to a climate shifting gradually from maritime to continental, with grape varieties and wine styles changing accordingly.
8.questions.1.question: What is the geographic relationship between the Vouvray and Montlouis-sur-Loire AOCs?
8.questions.1.options.0: Two Crus of the same vineyard
8.questions.1.options.1: Facing each other across the Loire: north bank (Vouvray) vs south bank (Montlouis)
8.questions.1.options.3: Montlouis is a sub-AOC of Vouvray
8.questions.1.explanation: Vouvray (north bank) and Montlouis-sur-Loire (south bank) face each other across the Loire, less than 5 km apart, with the same tuffeau soil and 100% Chenin Blanc, able to make dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling styles. Because Montlouis has smaller production and lower fame, its prices are usually 70–80% of Vouvray's, making it a good-value choice.
8.questions.2.question: What marks the boundary between Anjou Noir (Black Anjou) and Anjou Blanc (White Anjou)?
8.questions.2.options.2: Divided by a geological boundary (schist vs tuffeau)
8.questions.2.explanation: Anjou Noir and Anjou Blanc are "geological zones," with the boundary roughly between Angers and Saumur: to the west is Precambrian Brioverian schist (blue-black, hence Noir), and to the east Cretaceous tuffeau (snow-white, hence Blanc). This geological line determines many terroir differences, including Chenin style and the choice of red varieties (Cabernet Franc is more common in Anjou Blanc).
8.questions.3.question: Which of the following AOCs is the Loire Valley's only Grand Cru?
8.questions.3.explanation: Quarts de Chaume was promoted from its original AOC to Grand Cru in 2011, the only AOC in the Loire Valley to hold that rank. Coulée de Serrant, though of outstanding quality, is a "single-vineyard AOC" (like Château-Grillet) and not a formal Grand Cru designation. Bonnezeaux is a "Cru AOC" but carries no Grand Cru wording.
